lessons.intro: Missing the school bus or the Cairns coach usually comes down to one thing: a mix-up with time. Get comfortable switching between 24-hour and am/pm time, and working out how long a trip really takes, and you'll never be caught out.

sections.heading: 24-hour time vs am/pm time
sections.body:
**Am/pm time** repeats 1 to 12 twice a day. **24-hour time** counts straight through from 00:00 (midnight) to 23:59, so there's no mixing up morning and afternoon.

For times after noon, add 12 to the pm hour: 2:30 pm becomes 14:30. Before noon, the hour usually stays the same, just written with a leading zero if needed: 9:45 am becomes 09:45.

working: It's after noon, so add 12 to the hour

sections.heading: Reading a timetable
sections.body:
A timetable usually lists stops down the side and times across the top (or the reverse), showing when a bus, ferry or train departs and arrives at each stop.

Read carefully - mixing up a departure time with an arrival time is one of the most common timetable mistakes.

sections.heading: Working out duration
sections.body: **Duration** is how long something takes - the gap between a start time and an end time. A handy trick: count up to a friendly time first (like the next whole hour), then add the rest.

example.prompt: A bus leaves at 9:15 am and arrives at 11:40 am. How long is the trip?

sections.heading: Planning an itinerary
sections.body: An **itinerary** lists the legs of a trip in order, often with connections between them. When planning one, remember to include any waiting or connection time between legs - it's easy to forget and end up running late.

key_points: 24-hour time adds 12 to pm hours (after noon), so there's no am/pm mix-up.
Always check whether a timetable time is a departure or an arrival.
To find a duration, count to a friendly time first, then add the rest.
When planning an itinerary, don't forget waiting or connection time between legs.
lessons.try_this: Find a real timetable - a bus, ferry, footy fixture, or TV guide. Pick two events and work out the duration between them, writing the times in both am/pm and 24-hour form.

questions.prompt: In 24-hour time, 3:00 pm is written as 15:00.
questions.explain: 3:00 pm is after noon, so add 12 to the hour: 3 + 12 = 15, giving 15:00.

questions.prompt: What is 09:45 in am/pm time?
questions.explain: Hours below 12 in 24-hour time are the same hour in the morning, so 09:45 is 9:45 am.

questions.prompt: A bus leaves Cooktown at 06:45 and arrives in Cairns at 10:20. How many minutes does the trip take?
questions.explain: 06:45 to 10:45 is 4 hours (240 min). 10:45 back to 10:20 is 25 minutes less: 240 - 25 = 215.

questions.prompt: What is 18:05 in am/pm time?
questions.explain: 18:05 is after noon, so subtract 12: 18 - 12 = 6, giving 6:05 pm.

questions.prompt: The Isabella Falls swimming hole shuttle departs the info centre at 9:05 am and takes 18 minutes to arrive. What time does it arrive? Answer in am/pm form, like 8:22 am.
questions.explain: 9:05 am plus 18 minutes is 9:23 am.

questions.prompt: A junior rugby league match kicks off at 2:40 pm and finishes at 4:15 pm, including breaks. How many minutes long is the match?
questions.explain: 2:40 pm to 4:40 pm is 120 minutes. 4:40 pm back to 4:15 pm is 25 minutes less: 120 - 25 = 95.

questions.prompt: Nan wants to arrive at the Cairns hospital by 1:30 pm for an appointment. The drive from Cooktown takes 4 hours 10 minutes, plus a 20-minute fuel and toilet stop. What is the latest time she should leave Cooktown? Answer in am/pm form, like 8:00 am.
questions.explain: Total time needed is 4 h 10 min + 20 min = 4 hours 30 minutes. Counting back 4 h 30 min from 1:30 pm gives 9:00 am.

questions.prompt: A coach timetable shows: Cooktown depart 05:45, Helenvale arrive 07:05, Helenvale depart 07:20, Cairns arrive 10:35. How long is the stop at Helenvale?
questions.explain: The coach arrives at 07:05 and departs at 07:20. 07:20 - 07:05 = 15 minutes.

questions.prompt: A school trip leaves home at 6:45 am to catch a bus. The bus trip takes 2 hours 50 minutes. After arriving, there's a 25-minute wait for a connecting coach, which then takes 1 hour 35 minutes. What time (in 24-hour time) does the group finally arrive?
questions.explain: 6:45 am + 2 h 50 min = 9:35 am. Add the 25-minute wait: 10:00 am. Add 1 h 35 min for the coach: 11:35 am, written as 11:35 in 24-hour time.

questions.prompt: A ferry departs Cooktown at 22:40, and the overnight crossing takes 5 hours 45 minutes. What time (24-hour) does it arrive, and is that the same day or the next day?
questions.explain: 22:40 + 5:45 = 28:25. Since a day only has 24 hours, subtract 24: 28:25 - 24:00 = 04:25, and it rolls over into the next day.

questions.prompt: A coach timetable shows three trips from Cooktown to Cairns: Trip 1 departs 05:30, arrives 09:10. Trip 2 departs 07:15, arrives 11:00. Trip 3 departs 09:45, arrives 13:05. How many minutes does the shortest of the three trips take?
questions.explain: Trip 1: 05:30 to 09:10 = 3 h 40 min = 220 min. Trip 2: 07:15 to 11:00 = 3 h 45 min = 225 min. Trip 3: 09:45 to 13:05 = 3 h 20 min = 200 min. Trip 3 is shortest, at 200 minutes.

questions.prompt: A ferry timetable lists departures every 40 minutes starting at 06:00 (06:00, 06:40, 07:20, 08:00 ...). If Mia arrives at the wharf at 07:50, how long will she wait for the next ferry?
questions.explain: The departures are 06:00, 06:40, 07:20, 08:00. The next one after 07:50 is 08:00, which is 10 minutes away.

activity.title: Plan a real return trip with a connection, using an actual timetable
activity.why: Proves they can read a real published timetable and correctly work out total travel time including a connection - not one written especially for them.
materials: a real timetable with more than one leg (a bus/coach/ferry schedule, a footy fixture list, or one an adult writes out from a real schedule)
steps: With an adult's help, get hold of one real timetable that has more than one leg or stop - a bus/coach route, a ferry schedule, or a fixture list with more than one event in a day.
Choose a starting point and a destination that involves waiting for a second service (a genuine connection), or choose two consecutive real events and treat the gap as a connection wait.
Write down the exact departure and arrival time of the first leg.
Write down the exact departure and arrival time of the second leg.
Calculate the waiting/connection time between the two legs.
Calculate the total door-to-door time for the whole trip, from the very first departure to the very last arrival.
Record your results below.

record.label: Duration of the first leg, in minutes
Waiting time between the two legs, in minutes
record.hint: gap between arrival and next departure

record.label: Total door-to-door time for the whole trip, in minutes
Describe the real timetable you used and the two legs/times you chose

activity.check: total_trip_min should equal first_leg_min + connection_wait_min + the second leg's own duration. Ask to see the timetable if the total doesn't add up, or if the described schedule doesn't sound like a real published one.

lessons.title: Angles on a Line, at a Point and Vertically Opposite
lessons.curriculum_text: identify the relationships between angles on a straight line, angles at a point and vertically opposite angles; use these to determine unknown angles, communicating reasoning
lessons.intro: You don't always need a protractor to find a missing angle - sometimes reasoning alone gets you there, using three simple facts about how angles fit together.

sections.heading: Angles on a straight line
sections.body:
A straight line is exactly a half-turn, which measures 180°. Any angles sitting along that line, next to each other, always add up to 180°.

Think of a fence post leaning against a straight fence rail - the angle on one side plus the angle on the other side always makes 180°.

sections.heading: Angles at a point
sections.body:
A full turn all the way around a single point measures 360°. If several angles meet at that point, with nothing overlapping and no gaps, they add up to 360°.

Picture the spokes of a bike wheel, or slices of a whole pizza - however many angles are squeezed around that centre point, they total 360°.

sections.heading: Vertically opposite angles
sections.body:
When two straight lines cross, like an X, they form four angles. The two angles directly across from each other (not next to each other) are called **vertically opposite angles**, and they are always exactly equal.

Think of two straight roads crossing at an intersection - the angle facing north-east and the angle facing south-west (straight across from it) are always the same size.

example.prompt: Two lines cross. One angle is 40°. What is the angle vertically opposite it?
working: Vertically opposite angles are always equal

sections.heading: Putting it together to find unknown angles
sections.body: Real problems often combine these three facts. Work out which rule applies - straight line (180°), full point (360°), or vertically opposite (equal) - and always write down which rule you used. That's your reasoning, not just your answer.

key_points: Angles on a straight line add up to 180°.
Angles at a point (a full turn) add up to 360°.
Vertically opposite angles, formed when two lines cross, are always equal.
Always state which rule you used - that's the reasoning behind your answer.
lessons.try_this: Cross two rulers or straws on a table like an X, to represent two roads crossing. If you have a protractor, measure the four angles formed and check that the angles across from each other match, and that angles next to each other add to 180°.

questions.prompt: Angles on a straight line always add up to 180°.
questions.explain: A straight line is a half-turn, which measures exactly 180°.

questions.prompt: Angles at a point (a full turn) add up to:
questions.explain: A full turn all the way around a point is 360°.

questions.prompt: A fence post leans against a straight rail. The angle between the post and the rail on one side is 118°. What is the angle on the other side?
questions.explain: Angles on a straight line add to 180°. 180 - 118 = 62.

questions.prompt: Three garden paths meet at a single point, like spokes. Two of the angles between neighbouring paths are 150° and 95°. What is the third angle?
questions.explain: Angles at a point add to 360°. 360 - 150 - 95 = 115.

questions.prompt: Two straight bike paths cross at the lookout, forming an X shape. One of the four angles is 55°. What is the angle vertically opposite it?
questions.explain: Vertically opposite angles, formed by two crossing lines, are always equal.

questions.prompt: At a crossroads, two straight roads cross. One of the angles formed is 83°. What is the size of the angle right next to it, along the same straight road?
questions.explain: Angles next to each other on a straight line add to 180°. 180 - 83 = 97.

questions.prompt: Two straight fence lines cross at a corner post. One of the four angles formed measures 38°. What do the other three angles add up to?
questions.explain: All four angles at the crossing point add to 360° (angles at a point). The other three together are 360 - 38 = 322.

questions.prompt: At a point, three angles meet: 158°, 77°, and an unknown third angle. What is the third angle?
questions.explain: Angles at a point add to 360°. 360 - 158 - 77 = 125.

questions.prompt: Two straight lines cross at a point, forming four angles. One angle is 3 times the size of the angle next to it on the straight line. What is the size of the smaller angle?
questions.explain: Let the smaller angle be x, so the larger is 3x. Angles on a straight line add to 180: x + 3x = 180, so 4x = 180, so x = 45.

questions.prompt: At a point, four angles meet. Two of them are vertically opposite each other and each measure 70°. The other two angles are also equal to each other. What is the size of each of those other two angles?
questions.explain: The two vertically opposite angles total 70 + 70 = 140°. All four angles at a point add to 360°, so the other two together are 360 - 140 = 220°. Since they're equal, each is 220 ÷ 2 = 110°.

questions.prompt: Three straight roads meet at one point, making three angles that share the point (a full turn). The first angle is 110°. The second angle is 40° more than the third angle. What is the size of the third (smallest) angle?
questions.explain: Let the third angle be x, so the second is x + 40. All three add to 360: 110 + x + (x + 40) = 360, so 2x + 150 = 360, so 2x = 210, so x = 105.

questions.prompt: A student measures five angles meeting at a point as 60°, 70°, 80° and 95°, and says the fifth angle must be 60° as well. Using the fact that angles at a point add to 360°, is the student correct?
questions.explain: The four known angles add to 60 + 70 + 80 + 95 = 305°. The fifth angle must be 360 - 305 = 55°, not 60°.

activity.title: Measure a real crossing and test the angle rules
activity.why: Proves the angle facts hold for actual measured angles in the real world, not just angles drawn perfectly in a diagram.
materials: a protractor (or a phone angle-measuring app, or a paper set square for right-angle checks)
two long straight objects (rulers, sticks, brooms) or a real crossing outside (fence lines, path edges, roof lines)
steps: Find or create a place where two straight lines cross - two rulers or sticks laid across each other, or a real crossing point outside such as two paths or fence rails.
Label the four angles formed 1, 2, 3 and 4, going around the crossing point.
Using your protractor, measure each of the four angles as accurately as you can, and record all four.
Add angle 1 and angle 2 (two that sit next to each other on the same straight line) - check whether they add close to 180°.
Add all four angles together - check whether the total is close to 360°.
Compare the two angles that are vertically opposite each other (across the crossing, not next to each other) - check whether they are close to equal.
Record your results below.

record.label: Your measured angle 1, in degrees
Your measured angle 2 (next to angle 1), in degrees
The sum of all four of your measured angles added together
How close did your measurements come to the exact rules, and what was tricky about measuring?

activity.check: sum_all_four should be close to 360° - within about 10° is normal for a hand-read protractor. A total well outside that range (under 300 or over 400 wouldn't even be accepted) suggests one angle was misread.
